name: Fashion bible
about: Menswear rules, tips and example outfits, in the Smart Wardrobe app's vocabulary (garment types, colours, styles, fits and occasions as in app.js). Score an outfit with: sigmoid(model.bias + sum(rule.weight * check(rule))).

rules.title: Neutrals first, one accent colour
rules.why: Navy, grey, white, beige, brown, olive and black all go together; one brighter colour on top of them looks chosen, two or three look random.

rules.title: Three colours at most
rules.why: Past three colours an outfit gets busy and the eye has nowhere to rest.

rules.title: Mix light and dark
rules.why: Contrast between top and bottom gives the outfit shape; all mid-tones look flat.

rules.title: Tonal dressing works
rules.why: Shades of one colour from head to toe look calm and expensive.

rules.title: Classic colour pairings
rules.why: Some top and bottom colours are proven together: navy and grey, white and denim, olive and cream.

rules.title: Colours that fight
rules.why: Two loud colours of similar strength compete instead of working together.

rules.title: Keep pieces at one level of dressiness
rules.why: A very casual piece next to a very dressy one makes both look wrong; step at most one level apart.

rules.title: Dress for the occasion
rules.why: Being clearly under- or overdressed is the most noticed mistake; aim for the level of the room.

rules.title: Styles that suit the occasion
rules.why: Each occasion has its own vocabulary: tailoring for work, sportswear for the gym.

rules.title: Don't mix gym kit with tailoring
rules.why: Sportswear and formal pieces come from different worlds; together they look accidental.

rules.title: One story per outfit
rules.why: When every piece shares a style the outfit reads as intentional.

rules.title: Balance volume
rules.why: A roomy top looks best over slimmer trousers and the other way round; roomy on roomy only works as a deliberate streetwear look.

rules.title: One statement piece
rules.why: A big graphic, logo or loud piece needs quiet pieces around it to stand out.

rules.title: Go easy on patterns
rules.why: One pattern is easy. Two need clearly different scales (fine stripe with a large check), so most days keep it to one.

rules.title: Denim on denim needs contrast
rules.why: A denim top with jeans in the same wash reads as a uniform; pick clearly different washes or break it up.

rules.title: Shoes at the level of the outfit
rules.why: Shoes are read first: dress shoes with joggers or trainers with a tie break the look.

rules.title: Belt matches the shoes
rules.why: With leather shoes, the belt is in the same colour family: black with black, brown with brown.

rules.title: A tie needs a collar and long trousers
rules.why: A tie only works with a collared shirt and tailored trousers, never with a hoodie or shorts.

rules.title: Suits want shirts and leather shoes
rules.why: A suit is the dressiest thing most men own; a T-shirt or trainers pull it down to casual.

rules.title: The coat matches the outfit
rules.why: A puffer or rain shell over tailoring undoes it; an overcoat finishes a smart outfit.

rules.title: One metal for accessories
rules.why: Watch, rings and bracelet look tidier all gold or all silver.

rules.title: Dress for the temperature
rules.why: Too many layers is as uncomfortable as too few: about one warm layer above 24°C, three or four when mild, six or more when cold.

rules.title: Shorts only when it's warm
rules.why: Shorts below about 17°C look out of season.

rules.title: Ready for rain
rules.why: On wet days a jacket that sheds water and shoes that don't mind puddles; suede and white trainers suffer.

rules.title: Fabrics for the season
rules.why: Linen and seersucker for heat, tweed, flannel and corduroy for cold.

rules.title: Sports clothes for training
rules.why: At the gym, clothes made to move and breathe, and proper training shoes.

tips.text: Fit matters more than brand or price: a cheap piece that fits beats an expensive one that doesn't.
tips.why: Fit is what people notice first.

tips.text: Budget for a tailor: shortening sleeves and trousers and taking in a waist costs little and makes clothes look made for you.
tips.why: Off-the-rack is cut for an average body.

tips.text: A jacket must fit in the shoulders: the seam ends where your shoulder ends, with no dent or overhang.
tips.why: Shoulders are almost impossible to alter.

tips.text: A suit or sport jacket should cover your seat, roughly to the knuckles of your relaxed hand.
tips.why: Too short looks borrowed, too long looks dated.

tips.text: Jacket sleeves end so about a centimetre of shirt cuff shows.
tips.why: It frames the hands and protects the jacket cuff.

tips.text: On a two- or three-button jacket, never fasten the bottom button. On a three-button, the top one is optional.
tips.why: Jackets are cut to be worn that way.

tips.text: Unbutton your jacket when you sit down and button it again when you stand.
tips.why: It stops the jacket pulling and creasing.

tips.text: Trousers should have little or no break: the hem just touches the shoe. Slim trousers look best with no break at all.
tips.why: Fabric pooling at the ankle looks sloppy.

tips.text: The tip of the tie touches the top of the belt buckle.
tips.why: Shorter or longer breaks the line of the body.

tips.text: Match the width of the tie to the width of the lapels.
tips.why: Matching widths keep the proportions in balance.

tips.text: A pocket square should pick up a colour from the tie or shirt, not be the same fabric as the tie.
tips.why: A matching set looks bought as a kit.

tips.text: A buttoned shirt collar leaves room for one finger, no more.
tips.why: Tight collars pinch, loose ones gape under a tie.

tips.text: Shirts with long curved tails get tucked in; short, straight-hemmed shirts can be worn out.
tips.why: The hem tells you how the shirt was meant to be worn.

tips.text: A white or light blue oxford shirt works with suits, chinos and jeans alike.
tips.why: It is the most versatile shirt a man can own.

tips.text: Under a dress shirt, wear a grey or skin-tone V-neck undershirt, not a white crew neck.
tips.why: It doesn't show through or peek out at the collar.

tips.text: A fine knit over a collared shirt is a smart, easy layer; keep the knit thin so the collar sits flat.
tips.why: Bulky knits crush the collar.

tips.text: Knitwear should skim the body: hem at the belt, cuffs at the wrist bone.
tips.why: Too long or loose looks shapeless.

tips.text: A thin turtleneck under a blazer replaces shirt and tie for an elegant evening look.
tips.why: Smart without being stiff.

tips.text: Layer from thin to thick: tee or shirt, then knit or overshirt, then jacket, then coat.
tips.why: Thin inner layers keep the outer ones from bulging.

tips.text: Dark, plain, unripped jeans are the dressiest and most versatile; light washes and rips are casual only.
tips.why: Dark denim can stand in for chinos.

tips.text: Slim or straight jeans that sit on the hips without sagging work for nearly everyone.
tips.why: They balance most tops and shoes.

tips.text: Chinos in navy, beige or olive bridge the gap between jeans and suit trousers.
tips.why: They go with everything from a T-shirt to a blazer.

tips.text: Spend on shoes and keep them clean; scuffed shoes ruin a good outfit.
tips.why: Shoes are noticed more than most men think.

tips.text: From dressiest to most casual: black oxfords, brown oxfords, derbies and brogues, loafers, boots, clean leather sneakers, canvas or running shoes.
tips.why: Pick the shoe from the same rung as the rest of the outfit.

tips.text: Minimal white leather sneakers can go with chinos or a casual blazer, but not with a business suit or a tie.
tips.why: They are smart casual, not formal.

tips.text: Socks match the trousers (or the shoes); with shorts or loafers in summer, invisible no-show socks.
tips.why: It lengthens the leg and keeps the eye moving.

tips.text: Suede shoes are less formal than polished leather and hate rain.
tips.why: Texture lowers formality.

tips.text: Brown shoes with a navy or grey suit are a classic; black shoes for the most formal settings and dark suits.
tips.why: Brown is warmer and more versatile; black is stricter.

tips.text: A leather watch strap looks best roughly matching belt and shoes; a metal bracelet goes with anything.
tips.why: Leathers in the same family look put together.

tips.text: Keep accessories few and purposeful: a watch, a belt, maybe one bracelet or ring.
tips.why: Too many pieces compete with each other.

tips.text: Pick sunglasses that contrast your face shape: angular frames for round faces, rounder frames for square faces.
tips.why: Contrast balances the face.

tips.text: Colours with some contrast to your skin and hair usually flatter; colours too close to your skin tone can wash you out.
tips.why: Contrast frames the face.

tips.text: A simple colour split: about 60% a main neutral, 30% a second neutral, 10% accent.
tips.why: It keeps the accent special.

tips.text: Darker trousers with a lighter top is the easiest, most flattering combination.
tips.why: It grounds the outfit and lengthens the legs.

tips.text: When wearing one colour head to toe, vary the textures (knit, cotton, wool) so it doesn't look flat.
tips.why: Texture adds depth where colour doesn't.

tips.text: Earth tones (olive, brown, beige, cream, rust) all mix easily with each other and with navy.
tips.why: They share the same warm undertone.

tips.text: Black tie means a black or midnight-navy dinner suit, white dress shirt, black bow tie and black patent or polished shoes.
tips.why: It is a fixed dress code, not a suggestion.

tips.text: Business formal: a dark suit in navy or charcoal, white or light blue shirt, a quiet tie, dark leather shoes.
tips.why: Conservative colours read as serious.

tips.text: Business casual: chinos or wool trousers, a collared shirt or fine knit, optional blazer, leather shoes or loafers. No tie needed.
tips.why: Polished but relaxed.

tips.text: Smart casual: one tailored element (a blazer, a crisp shirt or wool trousers) mixed with relaxed pieces like dark jeans or clean sneakers.
tips.why: The mix is what makes it smart casual.

tips.text: As a wedding guest, never outshine the groom: avoid all-white, keep it a suit unless the invitation says otherwise.
tips.why: The day isn't about you.

tips.text: For a date or a night out, go one notch smarter than the venue: a good knit or shirt, dark trousers, clean leather shoes.
tips.why: It shows effort without trying too hard.

tips.text: In streetwear, build around one hero piece (sneakers, a graphic hoodie, a jacket) and keep the rest plain.
tips.why: The hero piece needs space.

tips.text: Oversized streetwear tops work with straight or tapered trousers; if both are baggy, keep the colours simple.
tips.why: Volume plus busy colours turns messy.

tips.text: Big logos look young and loud; quieter pieces with small or no logos look more grown-up.
tips.why: Let the cut and colour speak.

tips.text: Joggers and hoodies outside the gym look best when they are clean, well fitting and in plain colours.
tips.why: Sloppy sportswear looks like you just woke up.

tips.text: Train in proper training shoes and save fashion sneakers for the street.
tips.why: Support for the feet, and the sneakers last longer.

tips.text: A good T-shirt: sleeves end mid-bicep, shoulder seam on the shoulder, hem at the belt or just below.
tips.why: Fit makes a basic tee look intentional.

tips.text: A polo dresses up a T-shirt outfit instantly; wear it with chinos or shorts, tucked or untucked if short.
tips.why: The collar adds polish.

tips.text: An overshirt is the easy layer for mild days: over a tee, open, with jeans or chinos.
tips.why: Warmer than a shirt, lighter than a jacket.

tips.text: A coat should be longer than the jacket under it; a short jacket over a long blazer looks wrong.
tips.why: Layers stack from short (inside) to long (outside).

tips.text: A navy, camel or charcoal overcoat goes over everything from a suit to jeans and a knit.
tips.why: One good coat covers most of winter.

tips.text: Linen creases; accept it as part of the summer look rather than fighting it.
tips.why: Relaxed creases are the point of linen.

tips.text: Lightweight (tropical) wool suits work in summer better than polyester ones.
tips.why: Wool breathes, plastic doesn't.

tips.text: When combining patterns, vary their scale: a fine pattern with a bold one, never two of the same size.
tips.why: Same-size patterns vibrate against each other.

tips.text: A capsule wardrobe: a few pieces in neutral colours that all combine gives more outfits than many loud pieces.
tips.why: Every piece works with every other.

tips.text: Core menswear basics: white and navy tees, an oxford shirt, a grey or navy knit, dark jeans, chinos, a navy blazer, an overcoat, white sneakers, brown leather shoes or boots.
tips.why: These combine into dozens of outfits.

tips.text: Buy fewer, better pieces in natural fabrics; they last longer and look better as they age.
tips.why: Cost per wear matters more than price.

tips.text: Fold knitwear, never hang it; wash wool cold and dry it flat.
tips.why: Hanging stretches the shoulders out of shape.

tips.text: Rest leather shoes a day between wears and keep cedar shoe trees in them.
tips.why: They dry out and keep their shape.

tips.text: Wrinkled shirts and trousers look careless whatever their price; steam or iron before wearing.
tips.why: Crisp fabric reads as effort.

tips.text: To look taller: one colour from shoes to waist, no-break trousers, and fitted rather than baggy pieces.
tips.why: Unbroken lines lengthen the body.

tips.text: For a bigger frame: darker colours, vertical lines, structured jackets and plain fabrics rather than clingy or shiny ones.
tips.why: Structure and dark colours slim the outline.

tips.text: Take a hat off indoors; caps and beanies are casual only.
tips.why: Etiquette, and caps don't work with tailoring.
